headline: AI is screening your CV and consistently shows racial and gender bias, new study finds
summary: AI hiring tools, trained on historical data, often perpetuate existing biases, preferring white-associated names 85% of the time and female-associated names only 11%, even when names are removed.
details: AI models are increasingly screening job applications, scoring and ranking CVs before human recruiters see them. While marketed as fair and unbiased, nearly a decade of evidence suggests these automated tools often embed and amplify existing biases.

This isn't about a single faulty algorithm but a structural issue in how these systems learn. Models trained on past hiring decisions tend to recommend similar candidates, perpetuating historical workforce imbalances that anti-discrimination laws aim to prevent.

Machine learning systems are pattern-matchers; they learn from examples. If a hiring model is trained on a company's historical applications and hires, it identifies the "statistical signature" of preferred candidates, treating existing demographic skews as targets, not problems.

Amazon's 2018 experimental tool, trained on a heavily male engineering workforce, famously downgraded CVs with "women's" in them and penalized graduates of all-women's colleges. Amazon abandoned the project, unable to guarantee the system would not find other proxies for bias.

Despite advancements in large language models over eight years, recent research from the University of Washington in 2024 confirms the persistence of bias. Researchers tested leading LLMs with 554 genuine CVs paired with names statistically associated with different races and genders across 500+ job listings.

Across over three million comparisons, models preferred CVs with white-associated names 85% of the time and female-associated names only around 11%. Black men fared worst, with models preferring other candidates in almost every test, demonstrating systematic discrimination.

A crucial finding was that bias persisted even when names were stripped from CVs. Models, trained on vast human text, can infer identity from indirect signals like schools, cities, dates, or even specific word choices, still finding patterns lower down the résumé.
